system:
You are a computational scientist who builds mechanistic models of biochemical and pharmacological processes from experimental data. Work the way a careful scientist does:

1. Plan: call write_plan first with a short list of steps; update it if your approach changes.
2. Look before you fit: inspect the data and use run_python for quick numeric checks that discriminate mechanisms (for example rates by inhibitor level, dose-normalised concentrations, effect against concentration over time).
3. Retrieve: search the mechanism library and read the relevant cards. They give equations, data signatures, pitfalls and the library model name to fit.
4. Hypothesise: record at least two competing hypotheses with record_hypothesis, each with what it predicts in these data. Update their status as evidence comes in.
5. Test: fit competing models with the same error model and compare BIC, residual diagnostics and identifiability. Fit independent models in the same turn to save steps.
6. Revise: if every candidate leaves structured residuals, the true mechanism may be missing from the library. Work out what the data do that no candidate allows, write a custom model, and test it.
7. Stay honest: always consider the simplest model, including no effect at all. Report parameters the data cannot determine. Never state a number that did not come from a tool result.
8. Submit with submit_model, citing fit_ids (and card ids you read) as evidence.

You have at most 20 model turns, so be efficient.
task_prompt:
Initial reaction rates v (uM/min) of a purified enzyme were measured at substrate concentrations S (uM) (no inhibitor, I = 0). Each condition was measured in duplicate; rates carry additive measurement noise.

The data table has 16 rows with columns: S, v. Your model will be used to predict rates within the measured substrate range.

Find the mechanistic model that best explains these data, fit it, check it critically, and submit it.

Search mechanism library for enzyme kinetics cards
Fit MM and alternatives (substrate inhibition, Hill), compare BIC

content.thinking: The Michaelis-Menten fit gives a Km around 857, which means the data are nearly linear over this range. Velocity values at S=10 and S=20 suggest a slope of roughly 0.19. content.text: The MM fit pushes Km to ~857 uM with huge uncertainty, so the data look nearly linear over this range. I'll fit the linear and substrate-inhibition alternatives to test that.

content.thinking:
I'm comparing the models by BIC, and the linear one comes out best at -69.8 with a single parameter, so it's the simplest option. Its residuals against S are still weak at -0.148. Michaelis-Menten with Km around 857 behaves essentially linearly here, so there's no real curvature to find. The intercept at S=0.5 is small enough to sit within noise. I'm weighing whether to record the hypotheses and submit the linear rate model, with the caveat that these data can't tell it apart from Michaelis-Menten with a large Km.

I'm noting that the noise level is high, with sigma around 0.107 relative to some of the values, so the fit is only good enough for this purpose.

content.text: The linear model has the lowest BIC with one parameter, and the MM and substrate-inhibition fits collapse onto it (Km ≈ 857, Ksi effectively infinite). I'll record the hypotheses and submit.

input.evidence: fit1: Vmax=165, Km=857, both SE>270%; fully collinear; no better than linear. Saturation not detected in 0.5-20 uM range.
fit3: Ksi ~ 8.5e13 (no inhibition); rates rise monotonically to S=20 (3.8 uM/min).

input.mechanism: First-order (linear) regime, S << Km: v = k*S
input.prediction: Proportional rate with S across range; no saturation
input.evidence: fit4: k=0.190 (1% SE), sigma 0.107, BIC -69.8 (best of set), runs test z=0.07, no residual structure vs S.
fit2: n=0.98 (~1), K and Vmax divergent; reduces to linear; BIC -64.8 worse.

input.summary: Rates increase proportionally with substrate over 0.5–20 uM (v ≈ 0.190·S, fit4, 1% SE, BIC -69.8), with no residual structure. Michaelis-Menten (fit1) collapses to Km≈857 uM, i.e. the linear limit, and substrate inhibition (fit3) and Hill (fit2, n≈1) add no explanatory power, so the data do not resolve saturation within the measured range. Cards read: michaelis_menten, substrate_inhibition, hill_cooperativity (search results); first_order_regime card matched the linear model.
